section.title: Greeting to Gaius
section.sectionRationale: The letter opens with the elder's warm address to Gaius and a prayer for his whole-life flourishing, then names the thing that gives the elder his greatest joy: that Gaius is walking in the truth. This sets the key that the whole letter is played in.
section.thesis: Real Christian love flows through the truth: the elder prays for Gaius body and soul, and rejoices most of all that his beloved friend is not merely holding the truth but walking in it.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the address and prayer for Gaius; the joy of hearing that he walks in the truth.

units.label: The address and prayer
units.note: the elder to his beloved friend

verses.text: The elder, To the {{agapetos|beloved}} Gaius, whom I love in {{aletheia|the truth}}:
Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers.

units.label: Joy over a life in the truth

verses.text: For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to {{peripateo|walk}}.
I have no greater {{chara|joy}} than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

agapetos.gloss: Beloved, dearly loved. It is the elder's favourite word for Gaius, repeated in verses 1, 2, 5, and 11. The letter is soaked in warm affection; before a single instruction is given, Gaius is named as one who is loved, and loved in the truth.

aletheia.gloss: Truth, reality, what is genuine and trustworthy. In John's writings it is more than accurate ideas; it is the reality revealed in Christ, who is Himself the truth. The elder loves Gaius in the truth, and truth is the recurring drumbeat of this short letter.

peripateo.gloss: To walk, and by metaphor to conduct one's whole life. To walk in the truth means truth is not only believed but lived, step by ordinary step. The picture is of a settled, continuing way of life shaped by the gospel.

chara.gloss: Joy, gladness. The elder's deepest gladness is not in comfort or success but in seeing his spiritual children walk in the truth. It is a pastor's heart, measuring his happiness by the faithfulness of those he loves.

basic.context: This is the most personal letter in the New Testament, a short note from an old church leader, the elder, to a friend named Gaius. He opens with love and a prayer that Gaius would do well in every part of life, body and soul. Then he tells Gaius what makes him happiest of all: travelling believers have reported that Gaius is living out the truth.
basic.hermeneutics: It is a real letter to a real friend, so we read it as warm, practical wisdom for church life, not as a set of rules. The abiding point shines through: the elder measures a good life not by health or wealth alone but by whether someone is walking in the truth, actually living what they believe.
basic.originalLanguages: The word beloved, agapetos, sets the tone. Truth, aletheia, is the drumbeat of the whole letter. And walking, peripateo, means a whole way of life, not just holding right ideas. The elder's joy, chara, is tied entirely to his friends living in the truth.
basic.typology: Gaius walking in the truth is a small picture of every faithful believer who follows Jesus, the one who is the way, the truth, and the life. The elder's fatherly joy over his children echoes God's own delight in His children who walk in His ways.
basic.christ: The truth John loves is finally a person: Jesus, who called Himself the truth. To walk in the truth is to walk with Christ and to live the way He lived. The whole letter assumes Him as the centre and standard.
basic.god: God cares about the whole person, so the elder can pray for Gaius to prosper and be in good health as his soul prospers. And God is honoured when His people do not just know the truth but live it out day by day.
basic.crossReferences: 2 John is a companion letter with the same love of truth. John's Gospel records Jesus saying He is the truth. And Jesus teaches that we show our love for Him by keeping His word, which is walking in the truth.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's story moves toward a people who know God and live in His truth. This little greeting shows that story landing in one friendship: an old shepherd rejoicing that his friend Gaius is walking, step by step, in the truth revealed in Christ.

context.literary:
Third John is a private letter, and it follows the shape of one. Greek letters of the day ran sender, recipient, a wish for good health, then the business. The elder keeps that frame and fills it with gospel content. He gives no personal name, only a title, and he names Gaius at once, so the whole note is aimed at one man.

The opening is built on a small word that returns across the letter. The elder says "beloved" to Gaius in verses 1 and 2, and again in verses 5 and 11. He uses it as the hinge between the sections of the letter, so that each new topic begins with an act of affection before it asks anything. The word truth carries the other thread. It appears in verse 1 ("in the truth"), twice in verse 3, and again in verse 4, and it recurs in verses 8 and 12. Counting every occurrence, the letter uses it six times in fourteen verses, which is why it reads as the theme and not as a passing word.

Verses 3 and 4 work as a pair. The first is the occasion: brothers arrived and reported. The second is the principle that the occasion illustrates: nothing gives the elder greater joy than this. Reading them together shows how the elder thinks. A report of conduct becomes a statement about what matters most. The wish of verse 2 sets the measure, since it asks that Gaius's whole life go as well as his soul already does, and so assumes that the soul is in good order.

This section also sets up what follows. The brothers who testified in verse 3 are the same group who will appear again in verses 5 to 8, and the praise given here prepares for the warning in verses 9 and 10. The greeting is therefore not decoration. It introduces the people and the theme the rest of the letter will test.
context.historical:
The writer calls himself only "the elder." Early Christian tradition connects the letter with John the apostle, working among the churches around Ephesus in the later first century, and the letter's close likeness to 2 John and 1 John fits that. The text itself does not say, and the letter is best read as the work of one respected older leader writing to a friend.

Gaius was one of the commonest names in the Roman world, so the Gaiuses of Acts 19:29, Acts 20:4 and Romans 16:23 cannot be assumed to be this man. What the letter tells us is enough. Gaius belonged to a church within the elder's circle, he had the means and the will to host travelling Christians, and he was well known to people who moved from church to church.

The wish for health in verse 2 matches a habit of ancient letter writers, who commonly wished their reader good health near the start. The elder uses the habit but doubles it, praying for health and for success in everything, and then ties both to the condition of Gaius's soul. In a world with no reliable medicine, and with travel that wore people out, this was no empty courtesy.

The "brothers" were travelling Christians. First century churches were small households linked by messengers, letters and visitors, and a traveller's reception told the home church what was happening elsewhere. News of a believer's conduct travelled by exactly the route the letter describes: strangers arrive, they are received, they go on their way, and they report what they found. A good name was carried from city to city by people who had slept in your house.
context.canonical:
The words of verse 4 belong with John's habit of speaking of believers as children, which runs through his Gospel and letters, John 1:12 and 1 John 2:1 and 2:28. The elder speaks as a spiritual father in the way Paul does when he calls Timothy and Titus his true children in the faith, and Paul's boast of the Thessalonians as his glory and joy, 1 Thessalonians 2:19-20, sits close beside this verse.

Second John carries almost the same sentence in verse 4, which suggests the two letters were written about the same time and from the same pen, and that the elder was in the habit of reporting this joy. First John explains what the phrase means in practice. To walk in the light is the opposite of walking in darkness, 1 John 1:6-7, and the one who says he knows God but does not keep His commands is a liar, 1 John 2:4. The truth is something to be done, not only believed, a point John also makes in John 3:21.

The truth itself is traced to Christ. In the Gospel, Jesus is full of grace and truth, John 1:14, He says "I am the way and the truth and the life," John 14:6, He promises the Spirit of truth, John 16:13, and He prays that His people be sanctified by the Father's word, which is truth, John 17:17. Third John does not repeat any of this. It assumes it, and then shows what it looks like in one person's life.

The prayer for prosperity belongs in the long line of blessings for the whole person, from the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 to Paul's prayer that God would sanctify the Thessalonians completely, spirit, soul and body, 1 Thessalonians 5:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The elder wants Gaius to feel known before he is asked for anything. The opening is a deliberate act of friendship, and its warmth is part of the argument: the elder is about to ask Gaius to stand firm against a powerful man, and he begins by reminding him how much he is trusted and loved.

He also wants to set the standard before he applies it. Verses 3 and 4 tell Gaius, and every later reader, what the elder is looking for in any believer: a life that matches the faith. By saying this first, he makes the later praise of Gaius, the later rebuke of Diotrephes and the later commendation of Demetrius all measure up to the same line. Gaius would see that his own hospitality is being read as an outworking of this one thing, and Diotrephes would be judged by the same measure.

The prayer of verse 2 asks nothing odd of the first hearers. The elder does not suggest that outward success proves inner health. He says that he wishes Gaius's circumstances to be as good as his soul already is. The first hearers were meant to hear affection and a high estimate of Gaius's character, and to leave the letter encouraged to carry on.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The letter records what the elder prayed and felt. It does not command every believer to pray for money and good health in the same words, and verse 2 should not be pulled out as a promise of material success. The elder's wish is a wish, offered to one friend in a particular moment, and the rest of the New Testament shows believers who were faithful and yet poor, sick or imprisoned.

What the passage does prescribe is clearer when we look at what it assumes. A believer's life should be able to bear witness, so that when people speak of us the report is that we live by the truth. The elder's joy sets a pattern for how teachers, parents and pastors should measure those in their care. We can also pray for the whole person, body and soul, because God cares for both, while remembering that a prosperous soul is the thing that matters most. The healthiest application is a warm, specific prayer for friends, and a habit of rejoicing over their faithfulness.

debates.question: Does verse 2 teach that God wants every believer to be healthy and wealthy?

views.label: Yes, it is a general promise
views.case: Some teachers read the verse as a standing principle that God wills health and material success for His people, and they link it to texts such as Deuteronomy 28 and Psalm 1:3. They point out that the elder prays for both body and circumstances, and they argue that a believer should expect the same.

views.label: No, it is a friendly prayer and a conventional wish
views.case: Most interpreters read the verse as the ordinary wish for good health that opened a Greek letter, deepened here by the elder's love. It is a prayer for one man, not a promise to all. Paul himself left Trophimus sick at Miletus, 2 Timothy 4:20, and wrote of Epaphroditus's near fatal illness, Philippians 2:26-27, and Jesus told His followers to expect suffering, John 16:33.

views.label: It is a pastoral wish with a measure built in
views.case: Others stress the clause that the wish is measured by the soul's condition: the elder wishes outward life to match inner life. On this reading the verse commends care for the whole person without promising the result.

debates.bearing: The verse supports praying warmly for a friend's health and welfare, and it names the soul as the true measure. It does not support a guarantee of wealth, and the rest of the New Testament will not let us read it as one.

debates.question: Who is the elder?

views.label: John the apostle
views.case: The church has traditionally held that the author of the Fourth Gospel and 1 to 3 John is the apostle John, writing late in life from Ephesus. The shared vocabulary of truth, walking, love, joy and witness, and the closeness of 2 John 4 and 12 to 3 John 4 and 13, are the strongest internal arguments.

views.label: A separate figure called the elder
views.case: Some scholars notice that the writer never says he is an apostle, and they think a different leader, known as the elder, wrote the letters. They point to the early writers who spoke of an elder named John and treat him as a second figure.

views.label: An unnamed senior leader of the community
views.case: A third view makes no claim about identity and simply reads the letter as written by an older authority whose standing was recognised by everyone, so that the title itself said enough.

debates.bearing: The identity matters less for the teaching than the standing. Either way the writer speaks as someone whose word the churches were expected to heed, which is the very thing Diotrephes will refuse in verse 9.

study.originalLanguages:
The prayer of verse 2 uses the verb euodoo, "to prosper," which at root means to be led along a good road. It is used in Romans 1:10, where Paul asks that the way may be opened for him to come to Rome, and in 1 Corinthians 16:2, of putting money aside as one prospers. It is a journey word, so the prayer is that Gaius's whole path, not a single outcome, would go well. The same verb appears twice in the verse: that things go well for him as his soul goes well. The measure is the soul.

The companion word is hygiaino, "to be in good health." It is the ordinary word for physical soundness in the Gospels, as in Luke 5:31 ("those who are well"), and it becomes a favourite of the letters to Timothy and Titus, where it describes "sound" teaching, 1 Timothy 1:10 and Titus 1:9. The elder prays that Gaius's body will be as sound as his teaching and his soul.

In verse 3 the elder says he "rejoiced greatly," using the aorist of chairo with the adverb lian, "very much." The same phrase opens 2 John 4. The aorist presents the joy as a definite moment, the moment the brothers arrived. The participles "coming" and "testifying" are present tense, which paints a picture of regular visitors repeatedly bearing the same report. Gaius's good name was not one story. It was what traveller after traveller said.

Verse 3 speaks literally of "your truth," and then says that Gaius "walks" in it, using the present tense, which marks habit and not a single event. Verse 4 uses the present again for the children who "are walking." The tense matters because the elder is not praising a conversion but a continuing life.

Verse 4 has a double comparative. The Greek is meizoteran, a comparative built on a word that is already comparative, so it sounds like "greater than greater." English gets the effect only by stress: nothing greater. The grammar itself is a form of affection. The grammar of the whole sentence is plain and unadorned, and the plainness suits a letter between friends. Finally, "children" is tekna, the word of family and begetting, not of rule. The elder thinks of himself as a father and of his churches as a household.

typology.type: The prayer for body and soul together
typology.fulfillment: The elder's wish that a whole life go well points to the promise that God will one day restore body and soul completely, as Paul prays in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and teaches in Romans 8:23, where we groan for the redemption of our bodies. In Christ the healing of persons begins now, in the soul, and ends in resurrection. The type falls short because the elder can only wish and pray. Christ actually heals and, by His resurrection, secures health that does not fail. A prayer for prosperity becomes a promise.

typology.type: The father rejoicing in his children
typology.fulfillment: The elder's joy mirrors the Father's delight in children who live by His truth, and it anticipates the joy of the Shepherd and the angels over those who belong to Him, Luke 15:7 and 15:10. In Hebrews 2:13 Christ Himself says, 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me.' The pattern is escalated in Christ, who presents His people before the Father. It falls short because the elder's joy depends on reports and distance, while Christ knows His own fully and never loses one the Father gives Him, John 6:39.

typology.type: The travelling brothers who bear witness
typology.fulfillment: Brothers who arrive, speak and carry news of a believer's faithfulness anticipate the cloud of witnesses in Hebrews 12:1, and ultimately Christ the faithful witness, Revelation 1:5, who testifies to the Father's truth, John 18:37. The correspondence is that true testimony goes from person to person and builds up trust. The type falls short because human witnesses can be partial or wrong, while Christ's witness is perfect and the Spirit confirms it, 1 John 5:6.

study.christ:
The elder writes at the end of a long road. He once heard Jesus say, "I am the way and the truth and the life," and now he speaks of a life lived "in the truth." The letter never mentions Jesus by name, and that silence is a clue to how the elder thinks: by this stage Christ is so fully the heart of everything that it would be like naming the sun in a letter about daylight. 'The truth' means the whole reality of God made known in the Son, John 1:14 and 1:17, and so walking in the truth cannot be separated from walking with Him.

To see how deeply the thought runs, look at how John speaks of the Spirit. The Spirit is called the Spirit of truth, John 14:17, and He guides believers into all the truth by taking what is Christ's and declaring it to them, John 16:13-15. When the elder rejoices over a friend who lives in the truth, then, he is rejoicing over the Spirit's work in forming Christ's likeness in a person.

There is also a pattern of fatherly joy in Christ. Jesus said that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, Luke 15:7, and that He spoke His words so that His joy might be in His disciples and their joy complete, John 15:11. The elder's joy is an echo of this larger joy. The apostle who leaned on Jesus at supper learned that love for Christ looks like obedience, John 14:15, and he now finds nothing more satisfying than to see that obedience in others.

The passage also keeps us from a thin, disembodied reading of Christ's lordship. The elder wants health for Gaius's body because Christ took a body, healed bodies and rose in one. A Saviour who became flesh makes ordinary life, prosperity, health, journeys and friendship, matter. The standard for it all is still the same: a life that makes the truth visible. We should not turn this into allegory. The letter is about Gaius. But everything it commends is what Christ made possible and what He lived Himself.
study.god:
The first thing the opening shows about God is that He is concerned with the whole person. The elder, a man steeped in Christ's teaching, can pray for a friend's health and success without any sense of lowering the tone, because the God he serves made bodies, became flesh and will raise the dead. Spiritual life is not set against the physical. That is a quiet correction of any belief that holiness means disregarding the body.

Second, the passage shows that God's truth is meant to be lived, not only known. God is true, John 3:33, and His Word is truth, John 17:17, and what He gives He expects to bear fruit in conduct. The same God who reveals Himself in words wants those words to take shape in a human walk. This is why the elder's joy is expressed in terms of walking: God's truth has a direction and a pace.

Third, the letter reveals a God who works through people and their reports. The brothers come, Gaius is described, and the elder rejoices. God has bound the church together in a web of testimony, so that faithfulness in one place encourages believers in another. Nothing in the passage denies that God is the source of every good thing in Gaius's life, but He has chosen to make that goodness known through ordinary human witness.

There is also a tension the passage holds quietly. God is the giver of prosperity, yet the true measure of prosperity is the soul. The elder does not choose between the two. He wants both but knows which one is the standard. That is how the doctrine of God shapes prayer: we can ask God for health, provision and success, and we should, while keeping our deepest requests for holiness and truth.

For worship, this means that gratitude should include small, daily mercies and the faithfulness of friends. It also means that when we rejoice over another person's growth, we are sharing in God's own delight in His children, a delight that He has told us He takes in those who walk in His ways.

crossReferences.note: The elder writes nearly the same sentence to the church addressed in 2 John, rejoicing at finding children walking in the truth. The repetition shows that the joy is a settled habit of his, not a passing remark, and that the two letters come from one hand and one concern.

The report that gladdened the elder arrives by travelling brothers who give witness to Gaius. Reading verse 3 beside verse 4 shows how a particular story is turned into a general rule about what brings the elder greatest joy.

To say we share life with God while walking in darkness is to lie, while walking in the light brings fellowship. This is the negative side of the elder's joy: the truth cannot be professed without being walked.
Jesus calls Himself the truth, so the 'truth' that Gaius walks in is a person and not a body of rules. The elder had heard these words at the table and now applies them in a letter to a friend.
The Spirit of truth guides the disciples into all the truth. The elder's praise of Gaius presupposes this work: a life in the truth is the Spirit's fruit, not Gaius's own achievement.

Paul calls the Thessalonian believers his hope, joy and crown, his glory and joy. Like the elder, he measures his joy by the standing of the people he has taught, which shows that this is how apostles felt about their churches.

Epaphroditus was ill and close to death, and God had mercy on him and on Paul. This is a reminder that godly people fall sick and that the elder's prayer for good health is a prayer, not a promise guaranteed to every faithful believer.

Paul prays that God would sanctify the Thessalonians through and through, their whole spirit, soul and body kept blameless. This shares the elder's concern for the whole person, with the soul's holiness as the centre.

The one who delights in the Lord's law is like a tree planted by streams who prospers in all he does. The verse shows the biblical pattern behind the elder's wish, in which a life rooted in God's word bears fruit, though the Psalms also wrestle with the righteous who suffer.
Jesus tells the disciples He has spoken so that His joy would be in them and their joy would be complete. The elder's joy in his children is a share in this joy that began with Christ.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with people made to live in God's presence and walk with Him, Genesis 3:8, and it tells how that walk was broken and then restored. Adam and Eve hid from God's voice in the garden, and from then on Scripture traces the question of who will walk with God in truth. Enoch walked with God and was taken, Genesis 5:24, Noah walked with God in a violent age, Genesis 6:9, and Abraham was told to walk before Him and be blameless, Genesis 17:1. Israel was commanded to walk in all His ways, Deuteronomy 10:12-13, and the prophets mourned that the nation would not.

The answer to that failure comes in Christ, who is the truth in person and who makes it possible to walk as people never could. The Spirit is given so that the law written on the heart is truly kept, Ezekiel 36:26-27, and the church becomes the community in which the walk is lived out in company. Third John gives us a single frame from that story. One older believer hears from visitors that a friend in another town is living by the truth, and he is glad beyond words. In that small moment the promised renewal is seen as a fact: God's children, by His Spirit, walking.

It also looks ahead. The church is a people in progress, and the letter assumes both that faithfulness is visible and that it is fragile, since the same letter will turn to a man who will not hear. The story is not finished. What the elder sees in Gaius is a first instalment of the world to come, where the redeemed will see His face and His name will be on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4, and where nothing false will enter, Revelation 21:27. The joy of this one elder is a small picture of the joy that will fill that city.

Until then, the pattern holds: God tells us who He is in Christ, His people walk in it, and others hear of it and glorify Him, Matthew 5:16.

sermon.title: Walk in the Truth, Part One
sermon.why: From Begg's short series on 3 John, this message opens the letter, drawing out the elder's love for Gaius, the prayer for his prospering soul, and the joy of walking in the truth. A clear, orthodox handling of this greeting.

quiz.q: What gives the elder his greatest joy?

options.text: Hearing that his children are walking in the truth, living it out, not just believing it.
options.note: Verse 4 names this as his greatest joy, and walking means a whole way of life.

options.text: Hearing that Gaius is healthy and prosperous.
options.note: He does pray for this, but his greatest joy is Gaius walking in the truth.
The reports gladden him, but the joy is in what they report: a life in the truth.
His joy is entirely in his children's faithfulness, not in his own status.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Gaius walks in the truth?

options.text: His whole way of life is shaped by the truth revealed in Christ, lived out step by step.
options.note: The verb walk pictures a continuing manner of life, not mere agreement.

options.text: He believes all the correct doctrines.
options.note: Right belief is included, but walking means living it, not only holding it.
The travellers are others; walking in the truth describes Gaius's daily life.

options.text: He always wins arguments about the faith.
options.note: The point is a faithful life, not skill in debate.

quiz.q: How should we understand the prayer that Gaius may prosper and enjoy good health?

options.text: A warm, whole-person prayer, measured by the prospering of his soul.
options.note: The soul sets the standard: as your soul also prospers.

options.text: A customary friendly health wish shaped by Christian care.
options.note: True to the form of the day, though it understates the soul-first measure.

options.text: A promise that faith always brings wealth and healing.
options.note: This misreads a personal prayer as a guarantee; it is not a prosperity promise.

options.text: A sign that the elder cared only about material things.
options.note: He prizes the soul above all; the body is prayed for within that.

quiz.q: Who is the truth that runs through this letter, ultimately?

options.text: Jesus Christ, who said He is the way, the truth, and the life.
options.note: In John, truth is finally the reality revealed in Christ Himself.

options.text: The body of correct Christian teaching.
options.note: Sound teaching is included, but it centres on the person of Christ.
The truth is not private opinion but the revealed reality in Jesus.
Honesty matters, but that is not the deep meaning of truth here.

questions: The elder's greatest joy was hearing that his friend walked in the truth. What brings you your greatest joy, and how does that compare?
Walking in the truth means living it, not just believing it. Where is there a gap between what you say you believe and how you actually live?
The elder prayed for Gaius's whole life, body and soul, with the soul as the measure. How would your prayers change if your soul's health set the standard?
Gaius was loved in the truth by an old shepherd who prayed for him. Who has loved and prayed you toward Christ, and have you thanked them?
If travelling believers reported on your life this week, what would they say about the way you are walking?

translationNotes.note: The elder, ho presbyteros, is by long tradition the apostle John in his old age; the same self-title opens 2 John. In the truth can describe both the sphere of the elder's love and its genuineness.
Prosper renders a verb meaning to go well or have a good journey; combined with the health wish it follows a common letter-opening custom, here reshaped around the prospering of the soul.
My children is the affectionate language of a spiritual father for those he has helped to faith or discipled, as also in 1 John.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 3 John 1:1-4. The BSB combines the closing greeting into verse 14, so the book ends at 1:14.
